title: Introduce DRM subsystem and migrate graphics stack from fbdev
body:
# Introduce DRM subsystem and migrate graphics stack from fbdev

## Feature Description

Asterinas currently exposes graphics output through a basic fbdev-compatible interface (`/dev/fb0`). Userspace can `mmap` a single linear framebuffer and write pixels into it directly. This is sufficient for early boot graphics and simple framebuffer-based applications, but it is not the programming model expected by modern Linux graphics stacks.

The current fbdev path is fundamentally a fixed linear-scanout model. It provides direct access to framebuffer memory, but it does not provide a DRM/KMS-style device model with display objects, buffer objects, or atomic display control.

This model lacks:

- a DRM device interface such as `/dev/dri/card*`;
- kernel mode-setting abstractions such as connectors, encoders, CRTCs, and planes;
- userspace-visible buffer management primitives such as GEM-style objects;
- display update mechanisms such as page flip, vblank synchronization, and event delivery;
- modern permission and ownership semantics such as DRM master/device-scoped display control.

As a result, the current fbdev-based path cannot serve as a proper foundation for Xorg's modesetting path or for modern compositors, which expect DRM/KMS semantics rather than a single memory-mapped legacy framebuffer.

To support real Linux graphics userspace, Asterinas needs a DRM subsystem that can expose display resources, create mappable scanout buffers, and let userspace control presentation through DRM/KMS APIs instead of writing directly to `/dev/fb0`.

To successfully bring up Xorg (modesetting driver), Asterinas must provide a minimal but coherent DRM contract:

- a DRM device node (`/dev/dri/card*`);
- dumb buffer allocation and mmap capability;
- basic KMS support (CRTC + connector + mode setting);
- a framebuffer creation and scanout path;
- a page flip or equivalent presentation mechanism.

This issue focuses on reaching that minimal contract before extending toward full DRM feature parity.

## Goal

Introduce a DRM/KMS-based graphics path in Asterinas so that Xorg can run on a DRM device instead of depending on the legacy fbdev interface.

- Asterinas exposes a DRM device node to userspace;
- Xorg can start on top of the DRM/KMS path without requiring `/dev/fb0`;
- userspace can create and map scanout-capable buffers through DRM;
- display output is presented through DRM/KMS and remains stable during basic interactive use.

## Roadmap

### Phase 0: DRM mmap semantics
  
Before any buffer-object or dumb-buffer support can work correctly,  
Asterinas must support DRM-specific mmap offset semantics.  
  
This is a hard prerequisite for:  
- `DRM_IOCTL_MODE_MAP_DUMB`  
- any GEM-based buffer mapping

- [x] #3124 

### Phase 1: Minimal DRM Core and Device Model

Introduce a DRM core under `kernel/comps/drm`.
- device node: `/dev/dri/card*`;
- per-file DRM state;
- capability query;
- master/client capability handling.
- `simpledrm` drm device.

| IOCTL Name                 | Purpose                                                              |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `DRM_IOCTL_GET_VERSION`    | Return driver identity (name, version, date, description).           |
| `DRM_IOCTL_GET_CAPS`       | Query device capability flags.                                       |
| `DRM_IOCTL_GET_UNIQUE`    | Return the device's legacy unique identifier.          |
| `DRM_IOCTL_GET_MAGIC`       | Allocate and return a legacy DRM authentication magic value.               |
| `DRM_IOCTL_AUTH_MAGIC`       | Authenticate a client using a previously allocated DRM magic value.               |
| `DRM_IOCTL_SET_CLIENT_CAP` | Enable optional client capabilities (e.g. universal planes, atomic). |
| `DRM_IOCTL_SET_MASTER`     | Acquire DRM master for modesetting operations.                       |
| `DRM_IOCTL_DROP_MASTER`    | Release DRM master privileges.                                       |

- [x] #3127 
- [x] #3787 

### Phase 2: Dumb Buffer Foundation

Introduce a minimal dumb-buffer-based allocation path.

Provide:
- dumb buffer allocation via handle;
- mmap through DRM offset indirection;
- framebuffer creation;
- basic scanout compatibility.

| IOCTL Name                    | Purpose                                                      |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `DRM_IOCTL_MODE_CREATE_DUMB`  | Allocate a linear dumb buffer for scanout or CPU rendering.  |
| `DRM_IOCTL_MODE_MAP_DUMB`     | Obtain an mmap offset for a dumb buffer.                     |
| `DRM_IOCTL_MODE_DESTROY_DUMB` | Destroy a previously allocated dumb buffer.                  |

- [x] #3925 

### Phase 3:  KMS Object Model && Achieve Basic IOCTL Interface
 
Provide a minimal but coherent KMS object model so userspace can enumerate and inspect display resources.

| IOCTL Name                         | Purpose                                                     |
| ---------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `DRM_IOCTL_MODE_GETRESOURCES`      | Enumerate global KMS objects (CRTCs, connectors, encoders). |
| `DRM_IOCTL_MODE_GETCRTC`           | Query CRTC state (mode, framebuffer, position).             |
| `DRM_IOCTL_MODE_GETENCODER`        | Query encoder configuration and routing.                    |
| `DRM_IOCTL_MODE_GETCONNECTOR`      | Query connector status, modes, and attached encoder.        |
| `DRM_IOCTL_MODE_GETPROPERTY`       | Query property metadata (type, range, enum values).         |
| `DRM_IOCTL_MODE_GETPROPBLOB`       | Retrieve property blob data by blob ID.                     |
| `DRM_IOCTL_MODE_GETPLANERESOURCES` | Enumerate available planes.                                 |
| `DRM_IOCTL_MODE_GETPLANE`          | Query plane configuration and supported formats.            |
| `DRM_IOCTL_MODE_OBJ_GETPROPERTIES` | Get property values attached to a KMS object.               |
| `DRM_IOCTL_MODE_CREATEPROPBLOB`    | Create a property blob from user-provided data.             |
| `DRM_IOCTL_MODE_DESTROYPROPBLOB`   | Destroy a previously created property blob.                 |
| `DRM_IOCTL_MODE_ADDFB`        | Create a framebuffer from a buffer handle (legacy format).   |
| `DRM_IOCTL_MODE_RMFB`         | Remove a framebuffer and release its reference.              |

- [x] #3888 

### Phase 4: Xorg Bring-up

Validate that Xorg can run on the DRM device:
- legacy modesetting driver initializes successfully;
- framebuffer allocation + mmap works;
- display output is stable;
- basic rendering is functional.

| IOCTL Name          | Purpose                                        |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| `DRM_IOCTL_MODE_SETCRTC` | Configure a CRTC's display mode and framebuffer. |
| `DRM_IOCTL_MODE_DIRTYFB` | Flush modified framebuffer regions to the display. |

- [x] #3941 

### Phase 5: Vblank

Introduce vblank support:
- vblank event handling and synchronization;
- asynchronous event notification to userspace.

| IOCTL Name                 | Purpose                                |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| `DRM_IOCTL_WAIT_VBLANK`    | Wait for a vertical blanking interval. |

- [ ] #4032 

### Phase 6: KMS Atomic Modesetting Pipeline

Introduce atomic modesetting:
- atomic state representation;
- validation and commit pipeline;
- plane-based updates.

| IOCTL Name               | Purpose                                              |
| ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `DRM_IOCTL_MODE_ATOMIC`  | Perform atomic modeset or plane updates.             |

- [ ] #4051 

### Phase 7: Virtio-GPU Backend Integration

Add Virtio-GPU as a DRM backend.
- device discovery and transport setup;
- command submission pipeline;
- GPU-backed buffer objects;
- integration with scanout path;
- enable 2D acceleration.

- [ ] #4059 

## Additions

### 1.  DRM fbdev emulation

This provides a framebuffer device compatibility layer on top of the DRM/KMS infrastructure. It enables legacy userspace applications to access the display through a traditional `/dev/fb0` interface backed by DRM framebuffers.

### 2. Fix boot framebuffer pixel format

The current boot framebuffer initialization loses part of the information provided by the bootloader.

Two known limitations are:

- The pixel format is inferred only from bits-per-pixel (BPP), although multiple pixel formats may share the same BPP.
- The framebuffer stride (line length) is assumed to be equal to the visible width, while firmware framebuffers may contain padding for alignment purposes.

https://github.com/asterinas/asterinas/blob/dde91f0ccbe8d3fb0b239d2ed30da1053a3a8824/kernel/comps/framebuffer/src/framebuffer.rs#L73-L74

https://github.com/asterinas/asterinas/blob/dde91f0ccbe8d3fb0b239d2ed30da1053a3a8824/kernel/comps/framebuffer/src/framebuffer.rs#L90-L91

The boot protocol should preserve the complete framebuffer metadata, including:

- Pixel format
- Framebuffer stride (line length)
- Framebuffer dimensions
- Other firmware-provided display attributes when available

This would allow the boot framebuffer to accurately represent the underlying firmware display configuration and provide correct information for future DRM simpledrm integration.

- [ ] #3921 

### 3. Native Wayland Support

This enables native Wayland desktop sessions on Asterinas, allowing modern Wayland compositors and desktop environments to run without relying on Xorg.

The initial goal is to support software-rendered Wayland compositors, with future support for more complete desktop environments like COSMIC.

Related issue: #4070 

## Summary

The current fbdev-based graphics path is insufficient for modern Linux userspace.

To support Xorg, Asterinas must provide a minimal DRM/KMS implementation with:
- dumb buffer allocation + mmap;
- basic KMS modesetting;
- a functional scanout backend.

This effort depends on resolving DRM-specific mmap semantics and proceeds in a staged manner toward a usable DRM device, with further extensions (atomic modesetting, virtio-gpu) built incrementally on top.

title: Wayland support
body:
### Feature Description

Support native Wayland desktop sessions and applications on Asterinas NixOS.

Wayland support is an essential part of a modern and secure Linux-compatible desktop OS.

BTW I recommend natively supporting [COSMIC](https://github.com/pop-os/cosmic-epoch) desktop environment for validating Wayland support and becoming the default DE on Asterinas NixOS.

### Problem or Need

Asterinas 0.19.0 introduces substantial graphics improvements, but the documented desktop support remains based on Xorg.

X11's legacy security model provides weak isolation between applications: clients can generally observe input and interact with other clients within the same session. These limitations are particularly concerning for everyday desktop use involving browsers, credentials, and private documents, and they become unsustainable on an OS specifically focusing on security, like Asterinas NixOS. Wayland provides a stronger foundation by putting access to input, windows, and screen contents under compositor control.

Modern applications and desktop environments increasingly target Wayland, while the wider ecosystem is moving away from X11. Latest KDE Plasma drops support for X11 recently, after supporting Wayland for years.

Hardware acceleration would be desirable eventually. If a software-rendered Wayland session is feasible, that would already be a useful starting point.

### Suggested Implementation

Sorry I have no idea. Probably related to #2938 and #2008

### Possible Alternatives

Xorg remains useful for existing applications, but it does not address the need for a native Wayland desktop. XWayland could provide compatibility for legacy X11 applications within a Wayland session.

### Additional Context and Screenshots

The DRM work tracked in #2938 provide relevant context.

Given that you have good hypervisor support, Wayland support also makes using dedicated microVM for running GUI software possible, which significantly improves security and compatibility (cuz you can run Linux and even Windows applications in native environments). Currently there are mainly two solutions: [Google CrosVM](https://crosvm.dev/book/) and [cloud-hypervisor](https://github.com/cloud-hypervisor/cloud-hypervisor) with Wayland forwarding, used by [microvm.nix](https://github.com/microvm-nix/microvm.nix). They both support Wayland much better than X.

[COSMIC](https://github.com/pop-os/cosmic-epoch) is worth considering because it is Wayland-native, written in Rust with security in mind, combines a polished appearance with a relatively focused yet capable desktop experience. Related porting work in the [Redox](https://redox-os.org/) (a rust security-focused microkernel OS similar to Asterinas. Developed by a System76 employee) ecosystem also make it an interesting candidate for Asterinas NixOS. It is streamlined enough to be integrated into Asterinas NixOS. Its first formal release was in last year, and I have been using COSMIC daily for a year without any problem.

A working COSMIC session would be a meaningful demonstration of Wayland desktop support beyond simply launching individual applications. It can show Asterinas is suitable for daily use, not just a MVP.

I think Wayland support is needed. COSMIC DE support is my wish and IMO a good feature for Asterinas with reasonable workload once Wayland is implemented.

title: Tracking issue for supporting Asterinas kata in 0.19.0 release
body:
As of version 0.18.0, we have added support for using Asterinas as the guest kernel for Kata Containers. However, this support is still in a very early stage.

On one hand, we have applied a large number of patches on the Kata side — many of which exist solely to work around missing features in Asterinas, without a proper assessment of their impact on Kata itself. Some of these patches are likely incorrect and need to be revisited. On the other hand, several newly introduced subsystems have not yet been battle-tested under complex workloads, as they have only been validated against a simple demo case. We need more comprehensive testing to solidify stability.

This issue tracks the remaining gaps that still need to be addressed.

It is worth noting that production-grade support is inherently use-case driven. Different deployment scenarios may require additional capabilities. For example, we currently support the initrd-based boot method; however, if rootfs-based booting is required, we would need full support for ext4 and systemd — a flow that has not yet been fully validated. Certain scenarios may also require device passthrough support. That said, achieving full-featured Kata Containers support is clearly out of scope at this stage. For now, this issue focuses on tracking general gaps only.

- Network Support
  - [ ] #3222 （high)
  - [ ] #3224   (high)
  - [x] Support MSG_PEEK
- Virtio-fs improvement
  - [ ] Correctness testing (xfstests, high)
  - [ ] Performance benchmarking (fio, high)
- Boot time optimization
  - [ ] Add the boot time benchmark and optimize the boot time @cqs21 
  - [x] #3030 
- Audit and clean up existing patches. A key question is whether we need to support running multiple containers within a single VM. If not, weaker isolation on the guest side may be acceptable — after all, QEMU already provides an additional layer of isolation.
  - [x] Support mountable devfs/devtmpfs — currently, our devfs implementation hardcodes device paths directly in the kernel rather than exposing a proper mountable filesystem interface (high)@taosue 
  - [x] Mount propagation (MOUNT_SLAVE) (medium) @cchanging
  - [ ] `/sys/devices/system/memory` (hotplug memory use) (low)
  - [ ] PID namespace (low)
  - [x] `prctl(PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS)` #3552 
  - [ ] `/dev/mqueue` (low)

title: Ext4 support: Add basic writable EXT4 extent support
body:
# PR 01 Submission: Add basic writable EXT4 extent support

## Target

- Base: `asterinas/asterinas:main`
- Head: `HIT-HSSL/Asterinas-EXT4:ext4-port`
- Submitted head: `29b7afe5f8c9e0e3e9a2da76f762be7c8f5805a1`
- Recommended initial state: Draft

## Body

This PR evolves the existing EXT2 implementation into a shared EXT driver and
adds basic writable support for no-journal EXT4 filesystems that use extents.

This supersedes the earlier experimental PR #3581 with a commit history split
into reviewable architecture, on-disk inode, block-mapping, extent, integration,
and test changes.

## What this adds

1. Retains the existing `ext2` mount entry while adding an `ext4` filesystem type.
2. Supports 128-byte EXT2 and 256-byte EXT4 inode layouts with preserving
  writeback for unmodeled inode bytes.
3. Routes inode block operations through an indirect-block or extent mapping
  backend.
4. Supports extent lookup, hole detection, allocation, truncation, and reclaim
  for writable trees of depth 0 or 1.
5. Supports buffered file I/O and the basic linear-directory namespace
  operations exercised by the shared EXT regression suite.
6. Rejects journaled, indexed-directory, 64-bit, metadata-checksum, and other
  unsupported filesystem formats at the relevant EXT4 boundaries.
7. Preserves unknown compatible feature bits across superblock writeback.
8. Adds an EXT4 xfstests configuration and runs shared EXT userspace tests on
  both EXT2 and EXT4 images.

## No-journal durability scope

The no-journal implementation targets the same broad writeback durability class
as Linux EXT4 without a journal. A successful inode `fsync` writes the selected
inode's data, extent or indirect metadata, inode-table entry, and associated
allocation metadata, followed by one final device flush.

This does not provide transactional crash consistency or a globally consistent
filesystem checkpoint. A crash may leave allocation metadata and inode mappings
inconsistent and may require offline `e2fsck`. JBD2 transactions and recovery
are intentionally deferred to a later PR.

## Known limitations and open review issues

- Writable extent updates flatten the supported tree, update the complete
  ordered extent list, and rebuild the tree. This differs from Linux EXT4's
  path-based local insertion and node splitting.
- Writable extent trees are limited to depth 0 or 1. Operations requiring a
  deeper tree return an error.
- HTree directory lookup and mutation are not implemented. EXT4 filesystems
  advertising `DIR_INDEX`, and EXT4 directory inodes carrying `INDEX_DIR`, are
  rejected.
- JBD2, journal replay, unwritten extents, `fallocate`, 64-bit block numbers,
  metadata checksums, and crash atomicity are out of scope.
- Review identified an unresolved error path in extent-tree rebuild: if the new
  root has been installed and releasing an obsolete external node fails, error
  recovery can leave the published mapping inconsistent with allocation state.
- Review identified a remaining concurrency window in page-cache writeback
  error publication: waiters may observe writeback completion before the error
  latch is visible.
- Failure-injection coverage for data-range and obsolete extent-node release is
  incomplete.
- The current branch contains a temporary SDD report artifact under
  `.superpowers/sdd/`; it is not part of the filesystem implementation and can
  be removed during review cleanup.

This PR is submitted as a draft so that the architecture and commit split can
be reviewed while the open consistency issues above remain visible.

## Validation status

The earlier seven-commit head `fd14bf482` passed:

- per-commit formatting, normal OSDK checks, and ktests build checks;
- the complete KVM EXT2/EXT4 filesystem regression suite;
- EXT4 xfstests `generic/001`, `generic/002`, and `generic/005`.

The current head `29b7afe5` has passed formatting and diff checks. A normal
`aster-core` OSDK check was also completed for the compatible-feature change in
an isolated build environment. The current complete head has not yet completed
the container ktests build, KVM regression, or xfstests rerun; those results
must not be inferred from the earlier head.
